newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 14. [CORRECTED 11:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 14. [CORRECTED 11:30 GMT]

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- GRANDMET BOSSES' SHARE BONANZA

Directors of drinks giant Grand Metropolitan Plc could make multi-million pound gains by cashing in their share options early after the proposed merger with Guinness. However, because Guinness Plc would technically be taking over GrandMet under the terms of the planned merger, Guinness directors would not be able to cash in their share options in the same way.
-- BIG NAMES GO IN DMG RESHUFFLE

A reshuffle at the newly-created equities division of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell has seen two high-level executives leave the operation. The division significantly underperformed its first-year target, prompting the arrival of Mike Phillip as global head of equities. The bank has announced that Ian Wace (corrects from Weiss), head of equities trading, is to leave at the end of this month, and that his deputy, Steve Briddle, has also left.
-- BT 'BEING TOO PESSIMISTIC'

UK telecoms industry regulator Don Cruickshank has accused British Telecom of being 'too pessimistic' about the business it will lose to competition as a result of cutting charges to rivals. In an effort to avoid the cuts, BT had claimed that growth of exchange lines up to the turn of the century will slow to 2.5 percent to three percent, with the increase in call minutes down to 5.5 percent. Cruickshank has disputed the BT figures and instead predicted a 3.5 percent a year growth in the network and an increase in call minutes of between seven percent and 10 percent.
THE TIMES
-- PIA TOUGHENS DEADLINES FOR PENSIONS MIS-SELLERS

City watchdog the Personal Investment Authority (PIA) has published deadlines for 25 life offices and financial advisers to compensate some 550,000 victims who were mis-sold personal pension plans. The publicity exercise was accompanied by the threat of 'punitive' fines for those who fail to meet their timetable.
-- BECKETT SEEKS TO CURB HOSTILE BIDS

Margaret Beckett, the president of the Board of Trade, is reported to be considering proposals to make hostile bids much less likely to succeed. Beckett is understood to favour reform of the Competition Act in order to shift the onus of proof in hostile takeovers. Under the new measures, firms seeking control would be required to demonstrate that the success of their bid would be in the public interest.
-- ALLIED DOMECQ MAY FIGHT GUINNESS

Drinks and pubs group Allied Domecq has said it may object on competition grounds to the planned 24 billion stg mega-merger involving Guinness and GrandMet. The group's chairman, Sir Christopher Hogg, has set up a task force to look into the likely effect of the merger on markets in which Allied operates.
THE GUARDIAN
-- BT ACQUISITION SET TO CLEAR FIRST HURDLE

The European Commission is expected on Wednesday to approve the planned 13 billion stg acquisition by British Telecom of the US company MCI. The move follows an undertaking from both companies to abide by conditions aimed at meeting European Union anti-trust concerns. It is expected that the new group will have to provide capacity to competitors on its transatlantic submarine telecoms cables, and that MCI will have to sell off its teleconferencing business in the UK.
-- DRINKS DEAL 'DESPERATE MEASURE'

Institutional investors have reacted cautiously to the announcement of merger plans by drinks giants Guinness and Grand Metropolitan. Large shareholders are anticipating substantial disposals once the merger is completed. Fund managers, who welcomed the deal as the first in an expected round of takeovers and breakups, have described the deal as a desperate step by the companies to move forward in a difficult market.
-- ASTRA FIREWORKS TO BE WOUND UP AFTER BOTCHED SALES DRIVE

Kent-based fireworks company Astra is to be wound up, two years after a failed attempt to expand its sales through a supermarket chain. Creditors have appointed a liquidator to wind up the company, which has debts of 1.6 million stg. Following the failed sales drive, the company was left with 'considerable' stocks of unsold fireworks which needed repackaging and reworking.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- BAA TO BOOST INVESTMENT IN PROPERTY

Airports operator BAA is planning a major expansion of its property business. The move could see BAA, owner of Heathrow and Gatwick airports, quadruple its investment in rented office space and other airline-related buildings over the next three years. BAA is also thought to be considering a floatation of its fast-growing discount shopping centre operation, which it jointly owns with US factory mall specialist McArthur-Glen.
-- INTERFLORA TORN BY THORNY QUESTION OF WHO'S IN CHARGE

Interflora, the flower delivery association, is set for further boardroom upheavals following the events of the weekend. At an extraordinary meeting on Sunday, a board of rebel florists was voted in. However, the decision by the new board to shelve a promised postal vote on the ejection of the previous management looks set to be overturned, with the ousted board confident the ballot will return it to power.
-- ZENECA BUYS CROP DEVELOPER FOR 46 MILLION STG

Pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals group Zeneca has agreed to pay 46 million stg cash for the Dutch group Mogen. The company develops crops resistant to fungal diseases, and the move is in line with Zeneca's ambitions to become a world leader in genetic crop protection.
